Statements of what a learner will be able to do after completing a course, expressed as observable actions.

Example: "Analyze a dependency structure and diagnose its defects."

docs.title: Learning Pathway
docs.text:
An ordered route through material that respects what must be understood first, leading a learner toward a stated goal.

Example: One valid route runs from foundations through skills to publishing.

docs.title: Learning Record Store
docs.text:
A repository that receives and stores learner activity statements for later querying and analysis.

Example: A repository queried to find which simulations learners actually completed.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
A structured teaching outline for a single session, listing objectives, activities, and timing.

Example: A fifty-minute session with objectives, an activity, and a closing discussion.

docs.title: Level 1 Static Content
docs.text:
The lowest tier of textbook intelligence, consisting of fixed text and images with no navigation aids or interactivity.

Example: A printed page reproduced as an image with no links.

docs.title: Level 2 Interactive Content
docs.text:
A tier of textbook intelligence in which readers engage beyond passive reading through hyperlinks, embedded videos, quizzes, MicroSims, and a searchable glossary.

Example: A slider that redraws a chart as a reader changes a value.

docs.title: Level 3 Adaptive Content
docs.text:
A tier of textbook intelligence in which presented material changes based on a reader's demonstrated progress, using personalized pathways and concept-graph traversal.

Example: Additional practice appears for a reader who answered incorrectly.

docs.title: Level 4 Chatbot Integration
docs.text:
A tier of textbook intelligence in which a large-language-model-powered conversational tutor, often built on GraphRAG, answers a reader's questions in real time.

Example: A reader asks the embedded chatbot to re-explain a concept using a different analogy.

docs.title: Level 5 Autonomous AI
docs.text:
The highest, largely aspirational tier of textbook intelligence, in which a system deeply understands each reader's knowledge state and generates fully customized lessons in real time.

Example: A system regenerates an entire chapter's worked examples to match one reader's prior misconceptions.

docs.title: Linear Chain Detection
docs.text:
Identifying long runs where each idea depends only on the one immediately before it, which suggests missing relationships and a single rigid route.

Example: Forty ideas in a single unbranching line suggest missing relationships.

docs.title: LinkedIn Announcement Post
docs.text:
A short professional-network message announcing a book milestone, drawing its figures from the recorded measurements.

Example: A short post citing the book's page count and linking to the site.

docs.title: LinkedIn Carousel Document
docs.text:
A multi-page slideshow posted to a professional network, in which readers swipe through successive panels.

Example: Eight panels a reader swipes through summarizing a book.

docs.title: Listing Available Skills
docs.text:
Displaying the skills an agent can currently use, along with their summaries.

Example: A summary of every skill currently loaded and what it does.

docs.title: Local Development Server
docs.text:
A process that serves a site on the authoring machine and refreshes it as files change, allowing immediate preview.

Example: Saving a chapter refreshes the browser within a second.

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
The enumerated subject areas a course addresses, providing the raw material from which individual teachable ideas are drawn.

Example: Ten grouped subject areas from which teachable ideas are drawn.

docs.title: main.html File
docs.text:
The markup file defining a simulation's structure and loading its stylesheet, logic, and external libraries.

Example: It loads the styling, the behavior, and any external library a simulation needs.

docs.title: Marginal Token Cost
docs.text:
The additional cost of one more unit of output after fixed overhead is excluded, used to predict how expense scales with size.

Example: Roughly fifty-four tokens per additional glossary entry once overhead is excluded.

docs.title: Markdown Formatting
docs.text:
A lightweight plain-text syntax for headings, lists, links, and emphasis that converts cleanly to HTML.

Example: A chapter written as ## Section and - bullet renders as a styled heading and list on the published site.

docs.title: Markdown Parsing in Python
docs.text:
Extracting structure such as headings and fenced blocks from markdown source so content can be counted or transformed.

Example: Extracting every heading from a chapter to count its sections.

docs.title: MARP Slide Deck
docs.text:
A presentation authored in markdown and rendered as a self-contained web deck that can be published alongside a book.

Example: A chapter summary published as a browsable web presentation.

docs.title: Mascot Admonition Types
docs.text:
The distinct callout roles a recurring character occupies, such as warning, encouragement, or summary, each with its own visual treatment.

Example: One appearance warns, another encourages, and a third summarizes.

docs.title: Mascot Self-Introduction
docs.text:
The first appearance of a recurring character, in which it names itself and previews the roles it will play later in the book.

Example: The character names itself and previews its roles in the first chapter.

docs.title: Mascot Voice and Placement
docs.text:
The rules governing how a recurring character speaks and how often it appears, preventing overuse from diluting its effect.

Example: Two appearances per chapter keep a character noticeable rather than tiresome.

docs.title: Math Equation Support
docs.text:
Site configuration that renders mathematical notation from source markup into properly typeset formulas.

Example: A formula written in plain text renders as typeset notation.

docs.title: MathJax Configuration
docs.text:
The settings that enable and control mathematical typesetting on a generated site.

Example: Settings enabling equation rendering across every page.

docs.title: Measurement ID
docs.text:
The identifier connecting a site to its analytics property, placed in the site configuration.

Example: A short identifier placed in the site configuration to enable reporting.

docs.title: Mermaid Diagram Syntax
docs.text:
A text notation for describing flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and state machines that render as diagrams without manual drawing.

Example: A few lines of text produce a flowchart that stays editable in version control.

docs.title: Meta-Skill
docs.text:
A skill whose primary job is to route a request to one of several detailed guides rather than to perform the task itself.

Example: A single simulation meta-skill replaces seventeen separate generators while loading only the guide the request needs.

docs.title: Metadata Loading Budget
docs.text:
The cost of the always-resident summary for every installed skill. It is paid on every request, so descriptions must stay short.

Example: Fourteen skill summaries are read on every request, so each must stay short.

docs.title: Metadata Section
docs.text:
The part of a graph file carrying descriptive information about the work, such as title, creator, date, and license.

Example: Title, creator, date, and license recorded inside a graph file.

docs.title: MicroSim
docs.text:
A small self-contained interactive simulation embedded in a textbook page, focused on demonstrating one idea.

Example: A slider that changes a parameter and immediately redraws the result lets a reader discover a relationship directly.

docs.title: MicroSim Directory Structure
docs.text:
The standard folder holding a simulation's markup, styling, logic, data, metadata, and documentation page as separate files.

Example: Six files per simulation, each with one responsibility.

docs.title: MicroSim Generator
docs.text:
The meta-skill that routes a simulation request to the appropriate specialized guide and produces a complete package of files.

Example: A request for a chronology routes to the timeline guide automatically.

docs.title: MicroSim Index Catalog
docs.text:
A generated listing of every simulation in a book with preview images and links.

Example: A grid of preview images linking to every simulation in a book.

docs.title: MicroSim index.md File
docs.text:
The documentation page for a simulation, embedding it in a frame and providing a full-screen link and explanatory text.

Example: It embeds the simulation and offers a full-screen link.

docs.title: MicroSim Metadata Schema
docs.text:
The formal description of required descriptive fields for a simulation, enabling automated cataloging and validation.

Example: It requires authorship, discovery, educational, and technical sections.

docs.title: MicroSim metadata.json
docs.text:
The structured descriptive record for a simulation, covering authorship, discovery keywords, educational targeting, and technical requirements.

Example: It records that a simulation targets a cognitive level and needs one library.

docs.title: MicroSim Quality Score
docs.text:
A computed rating of a simulation against structural and presentation standards.

Example: A simulation with inline styling and no metadata scores poorly.

docs.title: MicroSim Screen Capture
docs.text:
Producing a still image of a running simulation for use as a catalog preview.

Example: A still image used as the catalog preview for a simulation.

docs.title: MicroSim Standardization
docs.text:
Bringing existing simulations into conformance with the current file layout, control, and metadata conventions.

Example: An older simulation is split into separate files and given metadata.

docs.title: MkDocs
docs.text:
A static site generator that builds a navigable website from a directory of markdown files and a configuration file.

Example: A folder of chapter files becomes a navigable website.

docs.title: MkDocs Material Theme
docs.text:
A widely used presentation layer for MkDocs providing search, navigation, admonitions, code highlighting, and responsive layout.

Example: It supplies search, callouts, and responsive layout without custom styling.

docs.title: MkDocs Plugins
docs.text:
Optional packages that add capabilities to a site generator, such as search enhancements or image handling.

Example: A plugin that generates social preview images at build time.

docs.title: mkdocs.yml Configuration
docs.text:
The file that declares a site's title, theme, plugins, extensions, and navigation tree.

Example: It declares the site title, theme, and the full menu.

docs.title: Model Selection Per Skill
docs.text:
Declaring which model tier a skill should run on, so demanding work gets a stronger model and routine work gets a cheaper one.

Example: Simulation generation is assigned a high-capability model while quiz formatting is assigned a lighter one.

docs.title: Model Versus Script Division
docs.text:
The design rule separating work that requires judgment, which the model performs, from work with one correct answer, which a program performs.

Example: Prose is written by the model; word counts are produced by a script.

docs.title: Multiple Learning Pathways
docs.text:
The property of a well-formed structure that several valid routes exist through the material, rather than one fixed sequence.

Example: A reader may reach publishing through either the simulation or the media route.

docs.title: Multiple-Choice Question
docs.text:
An assessment item presenting one correct answer among several alternatives.

Example: One correct answer among four, each alternative reflecting a real misunderstanding.

docs.title: Navigation Structure
docs.text:
The ordered hierarchy of pages presented to readers as a site's menu, declared explicitly rather than inferred from the filesystem.

Example: Every new markdown file must be added to this structure or it will not appear in the site menu.

docs.title: Never Use Master Branch
docs.text:
The project convention that the principal line of development is always named main, including in configuration that generates edit links.

Example: A configuration generating edit links must point at the main branch.

docs.title: Nodes Section
docs.text:
The part of a graph file listing every teachable idea with its identifier, label, and category assignment.

Example: Each idea with its identifier, label, and category.

docs.title: Non-Circular Definition
docs.text:
A definition that does not rely on the term being defined, nor on another term whose own definition depends on it.

Example: "A learning graph is a graph that shows learning" explains nothing and is circular.

docs.title: Nondeterminism in LLM Output
docs.text:
The property that a language model may produce different responses to identical input across runs, because output is sampled rather than computed deterministically.

Example: Running the same generation twice can yield two valid but differently worded definitions, which is why quality checks are scripted rather than eyeballed.

docs.title: Note and Tip Admonitions
docs.text:
Callout variants used for supplementary information and practical advice respectively.

Example: A tip box offers a shortcut without interrupting the main explanation.

docs.title: On-Demand Guide Loading
docs.text: Reading a detailed instruction file only at the moment the matching task begins, rather than keeping every guide resident.

docs.title: One-Shot Generation Risk
docs.text: The hazard of asking an image generator to invent factual content and render it simultaneously, since neither step is verified.

docs.title: Open Educational Resources
docs.text: Teaching materials released under terms that permit free use, adaptation, and redistribution.

docs.title: Open Graph Meta Tags
docs.text: Markup in a page header supplying the title, description, and image that platforms use when rendering a shared link.

docs.title: OpenAI Codex
docs.text: An AI coding agent from OpenAI capable of running skills that adhere to the portable subset of the standard.

docs.title: Optimizing Claude Usage
docs.text: Arranging work to fit within plan allowances by sequencing, batching, and offloading deterministic steps.

docs.title: Opus Versus Sonnet Routing
docs.text: The specific choice between a high-capability model and a faster, cheaper one, traded off against task difficulty and cost.

docs.title: Orphaned Node
docs.text:
A teachable idea with no incoming and no outgoing arrows, disconnected from the rest of the structure and indicating a defect.

Example: An idea added to the list but never linked to anything will appear isolated in the rendered diagram.

docs.title: Outdegree Analysis
docs.text: Counting how many prerequisites each idea declares, revealing ideas that may be too demanding to introduce at one point.

docs.title: Overlay Explore Mode
docs.text: An interaction style in which hovering or selecting a marker reveals explanatory information about that feature.

docs.title: Overlay Quiz Mode
docs.text: An interaction style in which a reader is asked to identify a named feature by selecting the correct marker.

docs.title: p5.js Built-In Controls
docs.text: The interface elements the drawing library supplies directly, used instead of hand-drawn substitutes so behavior stays consistent and accessible.

docs.title: p5.js Draw Loop
docs.text: The routine that runs repeatedly to render each frame, producing animation and responding to changing values.

docs.title: p5.js Library
docs.text: A JavaScript library for drawing and animation that provides a canvas, a render loop, and simple interface controls.

docs.title: p5.js Setup Function
docs.text: The routine that runs once at start to create the canvas and build interface controls.

docs.title: Page Feedback Widget
docs.text: A simple control asking whether a page was helpful, collecting signal about which material needs revision.

docs.title: Parallel Agent Execution
docs.text: Running several agents at the same time on portions of a task, paying startup overhead once per agent.

docs.title: Parts Kit Buildability
docs.text: The requirement that a practical activity be completable with an affordable, specified set of components.

docs.title: Passage-Level Verification
docs.text:
Confirming an assertion by quoting the specific text in a source that supports it, rather than citing a document as a whole.

Example: A figure is accepted only when the sentence stating it can be quoted from the cited page.

docs.title: Path Handling
docs.text: Constructing and resolving file locations reliably so scripts work regardless of the directory they are run from.

docs.title: Pedagogical Mascot
docs.text:
A recurring character that delivers guidance, warnings, and encouragement in a consistent voice, giving a book a familiar presence.

Example: A character who appears to flag a common mistake helps readers recognize a recurring hazard.

docs.title: Permission Management
docs.text: Controlling which actions an agent may take without asking, balancing convenience against the risk of unintended changes.

docs.title: pip Package Management
docs.text: The tool that installs and updates third-party Python packages.

docs.title: Pipe-Delimited Dependencies
docs.text:
A storage convention listing several prerequisite identifiers in one spreadsheet cell separated by vertical bars.

Example: A cell containing 1|3|7 records three prerequisites for a single idea.

docs.title: Plotly Library
docs.text: A JavaScript plotting library well suited to mathematical functions and scientific charts with interactive axes.

docs.title: PowerPoint Lecture Deck
docs.text: A downloadable presentation file intended for classroom use, generated with structured narrative and presenter guidance.

docs.title: Practice Exercises
docs.text: Problems a learner attempts without a shown solution, used to consolidate a newly presented procedure.

docs.title: Precise Definition
docs.text: A definition that states exactly what a term means without ambiguity or unnecessary hedging.

docs.title: Prerequisite Ordering in Text
docs.text: Arranging explanations within a chapter so nothing is used before it has been introduced.

docs.title: Prerequisite Relationship
docs.text: The specific pairing in which one idea must precede another, forming the basis of a recommended teaching order.

docs.title: Press Release
docs.text: A formal announcement written for journalists, stating what was released, why it matters, and where to find it.

docs.title: Progressive Disclosure
docs.text:
The loading strategy in which an agent sees only a skill's summary by default, reads its instructions when triggered, and opens detailed guides only when needed.

Example: A routing table of one page stays resident while a thirty-page implementation guide loads only for the matching request.

docs.title: Project Instruction Files
docs.text: The documents carrying persistent guidance for agents working in a repository, sometimes duplicated under a second filename for platform compatibility.

docs.title: Project-Local Skill Directory
docs.text: A folder inside a single book holding skills that apply only to that book.

docs.title: Project-Specific Skills
docs.text:
Skills installed inside one project so they apply only to that book, typically because they encode subject-specific knowledge.

Example: A circuit-drawing skill lives in the electronics book and is invisible to unrelated projects.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text: The text supplied to a language model to elicit a response. It carries the request, any supporting material, and constraints on the desired output.

docs.title: Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
The practice of composing and revising prompts so a model produces accurate, well-formed output reliably rather than by chance.

Example: Specifying "return only a JSON array, no prose" removes the need to strip explanatory text from the result.

docs.title: Pronounce Button
docs.text:
A small control beside a defined term that plays its spoken pronunciation, helping readers with unfamiliar vocabulary.

Example: A reader unsure how to say a technical term hears it rather than guessing.

docs.title: Prose to Circuit Translation
docs.text: Interpreting a plain-language description of a circuit and expressing it as an explicit component and connection list.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
A general-purpose programming language used throughout this workflow for parsing, validating, converting, and reporting on textbook data.

Example: A short Python script converts a dependency spreadsheet into the JSON format the graph viewer expects.

docs.title: Python Scripts in Skills
docs.text:
Programs bundled with a skill that perform its deterministic steps, keeping that work out of the model's output.

Example: A script counts words and equations across every chapter and writes the totals to a metrics file.

docs.title: Python Standard Library
docs.text: The modules distributed with Python that handle common tasks such as file access, structured data, and pattern matching without additional installation.

docs.title: Quality Gate
docs.text:
A defined check that output must pass before the next stage begins, preventing defects from propagating into expensive downstream work.

Example: A learning graph must contain no cycles before chapter generation starts.

docs.title: Quality Gate Short-Circuit
docs.text:
Skipping a validation step whose result is already known to pass, avoiding cost without lowering standards.

Example: A course description already scored above the threshold is not re-scored during a later run.

docs.title: Quality Metrics Report
docs.text: The generated document presenting structural measurements of a graph together with recommendations for improvement.

docs.title: Question Admonition
docs.text: A callout variant used to pose a question to the reader, often with a concealed answer.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text: A set of questions used to check whether a reader has grasped a chapter's material.

docs.title: Quiz Analytics
docs.text: Analysis of assessment results to identify material readers consistently struggle with.

docs.title: Quiz Bank JSON
docs.text: A structured export of all assessment items across a book, usable by external systems.

docs.title: Quiz Bloom Distribution
docs.text: The allocation of assessment items across cognitive categories, ensuring a quiz tests more than recall.

docs.title: Quiz Explanation Text
docs.text: The rationale accompanying each item that states why the correct answer is right and why each alternative is wrong.

docs.title: Quiz Generator
docs.text: The skill that produces chapter assessments aligned to assigned ideas and distributed across cognitive categories.

docs.title: Rate Limit Handling
docs.text: Responding to a throughput or allowance cap by pacing work rather than failing, so a long job completes across periods.

docs.title: Read-Only State Detection
docs.text: Inspecting a project to determine its progress without altering any file, so a status report can never cause damage.

docs.title: Reading Level Consistency
docs.text: Uniformity of textual difficulty across a book, so chapters written separately do not vary noticeably in complexity.

docs.title: Reading Level Specification
docs.text: A declared expectation of textual difficulty, used to keep prose consistent across chapters written at different times.

docs.title: README Generation
docs.text: Producing the repository's front page, including a summary, badges, statistics, and setup instructions.

docs.title: Reference Docs in Skills
docs.text: Detailed instructional documents stored alongside a skill and read selectively, allowing depth without a permanent loading cost.

docs.title: Reference File Separation
docs.text: Storing citations outside chapter prose so they can be reviewed and updated without loading the chapter body.

docs.title: Reference Generator
docs.text: The skill that produces curated citation lists for each chapter with short statements of each source's relevance.

docs.title: Reference Loading Budget
docs.text: The cost of opening a specific detailed guide, paid only for the one guide a task actually needs.

docs.title: References Directory
docs.text: The folder holding detailed guides that are read only when a particular task requires them, keeping them out of the default load.

docs.title: Regular Expressions
docs.text: A pattern language for matching and extracting text, used to locate structured fragments inside documents.

docs.title: Reinforcing Loop
docs.text:
A closed path of influence in which a change is amplified as it travels around the loop, producing growth or collapse.

Example: More users attract more content, which attracts more users.

docs.title: Remember Level
docs.text: The cognitive category covering retrieval of stored knowledge, expressed by actions such as defining, listing, and identifying.

docs.title: Rendered Image Audit
docs.text: Checking a finished picture against its locked specification to confirm every element was reproduced correctly.

docs.title: Repository Badges
docs.text: Small status images displayed on a repository page showing license, build state, or site link.

docs.title: Responsive Sim Layout
docs.text: Designing a simulation so it adapts to the width available, remaining usable on narrow screens and inside frames.

docs.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
docs.text:
A technique in which relevant stored passages are retrieved and supplied to a model so its answers are grounded in specific source material.

Example: A course assistant answers from the book's own exported question set rather than from general knowledge.

docs.title: Runbook Command
docs.text:
A command that reports the ordered steps of a process and identifies which step comes next, without performing the steps itself.

Example: A runbook reports that the learning graph exists and the chapter structure does not, so chapter design is next.

docs.title: Runnable Code Block
docs.text: A code sample a reader can execute in place and modify, rather than only read.

docs.title: Schematic Verification
docs.text: Confirming that a rendered electrical diagram matches the circuit that was described.

docs.title: Schemdraw Library
docs.text:
A Python library that draws electrical schematics from code, so a diagram remains editable and version-controlled.

Example: A schematic is stored as a short program, letting a component value change without redrawing anything by hand.

docs.title: Script Execution Permissions
docs.text: The settings that determine whether an agent may run a program directly or must request approval first.

docs.title: Script Exit Codes
docs.text: Numeric values a program returns to indicate success or the kind of failure, allowing other scripts to react.

docs.title: script.js File
docs.text: The file holding all of a simulation's behavior, including event handling and rendering logic.

docs.title: Scripts Directory
docs.text: The folder holding executable programs a skill runs to perform deterministic work.

docs.title: Search Configuration
docs.text: The settings controlling how a site indexes its content and presents matches to a reader.

docs.title: Search Metadata Section
docs.text: The part of a simulation's descriptive record holding tags, visualization type, and keywords that support discovery.

docs.title: Section Organization
docs.text: Dividing a chapter into ordered subsections so material progresses from simpler to more demanding.

docs.title: Security in Skill Execution
docs.text: The practices that keep a skill from taking damaging or unauthorized actions, including restricting tools and reviewing what a script does before running it.

docs.title: Seeded Randomness
docs.text:
Generating apparently random values from a fixed starting number so a simulation produces identical results each time it runs.

Example: A scattered arrangement looks arbitrary but appears the same for every reader, making it safe to describe in surrounding text.

docs.title: Selective File Reading
docs.text: Loading only the portion of a file relevant to the current task rather than its entire contents.

docs.title: Self-Dependency Check
docs.text: Verifying that no idea lists itself as its own prerequisite.

docs.title: Separate Quiz Files
docs.text: Storing each chapter's assessment in its own file so quizzes can be revised without reading the chapter body.

docs.title: Separate References Files
docs.text: Storing each chapter's citations in a dedicated file so reference maintenance does not require loading chapter prose.

docs.title: Separating Facts From Pixels
docs.text: The design rule that content is decided and verified in text before any picture is produced, so the image generator never chooses a figure.

docs.title: Sequential Sim Execution
docs.text: Generating simulations one after another by default, since concurrent generation multiplies fixed overhead without improving results.

docs.title: Serial Agent Execution
docs.text: Running one agent that completes an entire task, paying startup overhead only once.

docs.title: Serial Versus Parallel Tradeoff
docs.text:
The decision between finishing sooner and spending less. Parallelism reduces elapsed time but multiplies fixed overhead, and is only justified when the work is genuinely large per agent.

Example: Four agents writing glossary definitions cost more than twice as much as one agent and produce no better result.

docs.title: Session Log Format
docs.text: The agreed structure of a working record, covering the request, the choices made, the revisions applied, and the result.

docs.title: Session Logging
docs.text: Recording what was produced during a working session and the decisions that shaped it.

docs.title: Shebang Line
docs.text: The first line of a script that names the interpreter to run it, allowing the file to be executed directly.

docs.title: Shell Script Wrapper
docs.text: A short shell program that supplies standard arguments and paths to a longer program, giving it a simple name users can remember.

docs.title: Shell Scripting
docs.text:
Writing sequences of shell commands into an executable file so a multi-step task can be repeated identically.

Example: A script that starts a local server, waits for rendering, and captures a screenshot removes three manual steps.

docs.title: Sim Lifecycle Status
docs.text: The recorded stage of a simulation's production, progressing from specified through scaffolded, implemented, validated, and deployed.

docs.title: Sim Scaffolding Workflow
docs.text: Creating a simulation's directory and placeholder files automatically so only the behavior file requires authoring.

docs.title: Site Build Command
docs.text: The instruction that renders markdown sources into a complete static website.

docs.title: Site Logo and Favicon
docs.text: The small identifying marks shown in a site header and browser tab, typically derived from a book's cover or character artwork.

docs.title: Site Metrics Collection
docs.text: Gathering counts of published pages, simulations, and assets from a built site.

docs.title: Skill Alias Map
docs.text: A record of which former skill names now correspond to which routes inside a consolidated skill, so older references remain resolvable.

docs.title: Skill Benchmarking
docs.text: Measuring a skill's output quality, runtime, and token consumption against a fixed set of cases so revisions can be compared.

docs.title: Skill Composition
docs.text:
Combining several skills in sequence so the output of one becomes the input of the next.

Example: The concept list produced by the graph skill becomes the term list consumed by the glossary skill.

docs.title: Skill Consolidation
docs.text: Merging several related skills into one router plus a set of guides, reducing the number of installed skills without losing capability.

docs.title: Skill Creator Skill
docs.text: A skill used to author, revise, and evaluate other skills, including testing how reliably their descriptions trigger.

docs.title: Skill Description Field
docs.text:
The required summary stating what a skill does and when it should be used. It is the text an agent matches a request against.

Example: A description that lists concrete trigger phrases fires reliably; a vague one is skipped or misfires.

docs.title: Skill Directory Structure
docs.text: The folder layout of a skill: the required instruction file plus optional folders for reference documents, executable scripts, and templates.

docs.title: Skill Discoverability
docs.text: The degree to which an agent can determine that a relevant skill exists, governed almost entirely by description quality.

docs.title: Skill Distribution Methods
docs.text: The ways a skill reaches other users: a shared repository, a copied folder, or a plugin registry.

docs.title: Skill Evaluation Harness
docs.text: A repeatable test setup that runs a skill against known inputs and scores the output, making quality changes measurable rather than anecdotal.

docs.title: Skill Execution Context
docs.text: The environment in which a skill runs, including the working directory, available tools, and granted permissions.

docs.title: Skill Failure Modes
docs.text: The recurring ways a skill breaks: failing to trigger, triggering wrongly, loading the wrong guide, or producing output that fails validation.

docs.title: Skill Library
docs.text: The complete collection of skills available to an agent, together with the conventions that keep them consistent.

docs.title: Skill Library Maintenance
docs.text: The ongoing work of updating, testing, and pruning a collection of skills so they remain accurate as tools and standards change.

docs.title: Skill License Field
docs.text: An optional metadata entry naming the terms under which a skill may be used or redistributed.

docs.title: Skill Metadata Field
docs.text: An optional map of string keys and values carrying client-specific or organization-specific information that the agent itself ignores.

docs.title: Skill Name Field
docs.text: The required identifier for a skill, restricted to lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens, and matching the folder that contains it.

docs.title: Skill Naming Conventions
docs.text: The rules governing skill identifiers: lowercase, hyphen-separated, descriptive, and identical to the containing folder name.

docs.title: Skill Packaging
docs.text: Assembling a skill's instruction file, scripts, references, and assets into a self-contained folder that can be copied or shared.

docs.title: Skill Portability
docs.text: The degree to which a skill written for one agent platform runs correctly on others without modification.

docs.title: Skill Routing Table
docs.text: The decision table inside a meta-skill that maps trigger keywords to the guide file responsible for each variant of a task.

docs.title: Skill Testing and Debugging
docs.text: Exercising a skill against representative requests and diagnosing the cause when its behavior differs from what its instructions specify.

docs.title: Skill Trigger Matching
docs.text: The process by which an agent compares an incoming request against installed skill descriptions to decide which skill to load.

docs.title: Skill Usage Analytics
docs.text: Processing recorded usage events to reveal which skills run most often and what each consumes.

docs.title: Skill Usage Hook
docs.text: A configured callback that records information each time a skill runs, producing data for later analysis.

docs.title: Skill Usage Report
docs.text: A generated summary showing which skills ran, how long they took, and what they consumed.

docs.title: Skill Variance Analysis
docs.text:
Running the same case repeatedly to measure how much a skill's output changes between runs, distinguishing real improvement from random fluctuation.

Example: A skill scoring 80 once and 60 the next time has a consistency problem, not a quality problem.

docs.title: Skill Versioning
docs.text: Recording a revision number inside a skill so behavior changes can be tracked and defects traced to a specific revision.

docs.title: Skill Workflow Instructions
docs.text: The step-by-step body of a skill file that an agent follows once the skill is triggered.

docs.title: SKILL.md File
docs.text: The required markdown file at the root of a skill folder, containing metadata at the top and workflow instructions below.

docs.title: Skills Versus Commands
docs.text: The distinction between a capability an agent selects automatically based on a request and a procedure the user invokes explicitly by name.

docs.title: Skills Versus Prompts
docs.text: The distinction between a reusable packaged capability with supporting files and a single request typed into a session.

docs.title: Slash Command Invocation
docs.text: Triggering a skill or command by typing its name after a forward slash rather than describing the task in prose.

docs.title: Slide Deck Publishing
docs.text: Adding a rendered presentation to a site so it can be viewed in a browser and linked directly.

docs.title: Slider Control
docs.text: A draggable interface element for selecting a value from a continuous range, used for parameters such as speed or size.

docs.title: Social Media Preview Card
docs.text: The image and text a platform displays when a link to a page is shared.

docs.title: Solderless Breadboard
docs.text: A reusable board with gridded holes that hold components and wires, allowing circuits to be assembled without permanent joins.

docs.title: Source Discovery Phase
docs.text: The stage locating authoritative material that could support each planned assertion.

docs.title: Source Sidecar File
docs.text: A companion file stored beside a finished image recording every claim, its source address, and its supporting quotation.

docs.title: Speaker Notes
docs.text: Presenter-facing text attached to a slide, describing what to say and which points to emphasize.

docs.title: Stale Symlink Cleanup
docs.text: Removing filesystem pointers that reference deleted or renamed skills, preventing load errors.

docs.title: Stop Hook
docs.text:
A callback that fires when an agent finishes a turn, commonly used to record results or perform cleanup.

Example: A stop hook commits the turn's file changes using a message the agent left behind.

docs.title: Strict Build Mode
docs.text:
A build setting that treats warnings such as broken links as failures, preventing defective sites from being published.

Example: A link to a page that was renamed fails the build instead of reaching readers.

docs.title: style.css File
docs.text: The file holding all of a simulation's presentation rules, kept separate from its structure and behavior.

docs.title: Sub-Agent Startup Overhead
docs.text:
The fixed token cost of launching an additional agent, incurred before it performs any useful work, because it must receive its own instructions and tool definitions.

Example: Roughly twelve thousand tokens are consumed by each additional agent before it writes a single definition.

docs.title: Substitution Prohibition
docs.text: The explicit instruction forbidding an image generator from altering figures, names, or labels, or inventing additional ones.

docs.title: Supplementary Content
docs.text: Material surrounding the chapters, including glossary, questions, assessments, references, and reports.

docs.title: Supporting Assets in Skills
docs.text: Non-instruction files bundled with a skill, such as schemas, stylesheets, or starter templates, that its workflow copies or reads.

docs.title: Symbolic Link Installation
docs.text:
Installing a skill by creating a filesystem pointer to its source folder, so edits to the source take effect immediately without copying.

Example: Linking a repository folder into the agent's skills directory means a fix committed once is live everywhere.

docs.title: sync-iframe-heights.py
docs.text: The program that reads each simulation's recorded height and updates every embedding frame to match.

docs.title: System Prompt
docs.text: Instructions supplied to a model separately from the user request that establish persistent role, constraints, and available tools for a session.

docs.title: Systems Archetype
docs.text: A recurring pattern of interacting loops that appears across many different domains and produces a characteristic behavior.

docs.title: Target Audience Definition
docs.text:
An explicit statement of who a course is written for, which governs vocabulary, assumed background, and example complexity.

Example: Naming "professional development for educators" rather than "anyone interested" sets a usable writing standard.

docs.title: Taxonomy Category Naming
docs.text: Choosing descriptive category names that communicate their contents to a reader rather than only to the system.

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text: The count and percentage of ideas falling into each category, used to detect imbalance.

docs.title: taxonomy-distribution.py
docs.text: The program that counts ideas per category and writes a distribution report, flagging categories that exceed the share threshold.

docs.title: taxonomy-names.json File
docs.text:
The mapping from short category abbreviations to human-readable names, required so reports and diagram legends display meaningful labels.

Example: Without it, a legend shows LGRAPH instead of "Learning Graphs".

docs.title: TaxonomyID
docs.text: A short uppercase abbreviation identifying a category, used in the data files and as the group key in a rendered diagram.

docs.title: Technical Metadata Section
docs.text: The part of a simulation's descriptive record holding framework, dimensions, dependencies, and accessibility information.

docs.title: Template Files in Skills
docs.text: Prewritten starter files a skill copies into a project and then customizes, avoiding regeneration of boilerplate.

docs.title: Term Extraction
docs.text: Identifying the vocabulary requiring definition, drawn from an enumerated idea list and from wording used across the written material.

docs.title: Terminal Commands
docs.text: Text instructions typed at a command-line shell to run programs, inspect files, and manage a project.

docs.title: Terminal Node
docs.text: A teachable idea that has prerequisites but that nothing else depends on, representing a natural endpoint of a route.

docs.title: Text Input Control
docs.text: An interface element accepting typed values, used where a reader supplies a number or short string.

docs.title: Text Rendering in Images
docs.text: The capability of an image generator to draw legible, exact wording inside a picture, which makes designed posters feasible and mistakes permanent.

docs.title: Text-to-Image Model
docs.text: A generative system that produces a picture from a written description, including modern systems able to place specified text accurately within a complex composition.

docs.title: Text-to-Speech Narration
docs.text: Generated spoken audio of written material, offering an alternative to reading.

docs.title: Textbook Generation Pipeline
docs.text: The ordered sequence of steps that turns a course description into a published book, passing through concepts, structure, content, media, and deployment.

docs.title: Textbook Scaffold
docs.text: The initial project structure created for a new book, including configuration, directory layout, and starter pages.

docs.title: Thirty Skill Loading Limit
docs.text: The practical ceiling on how many skills an agent can keep available at once, which forces related skills to be consolidated.

docs.title: Title Case Convention
docs.text: The capitalization rule applying initial capitals to principal words, used for consistency across labels and headings.

docs.title: TODO Backlog Generation
docs.text: Producing a consolidated list of outstanding work items across a project from automated assessments.

docs.title: Token
docs.text:
The smallest unit of text a language model processes, roughly equivalent to a short word or word fragment. Model cost and capacity are measured in tokens rather than words.

Example: The phrase "learning graph" is typically three or four tokens, not two words.

docs.title: Token Budget
docs.text:
A planned allowance of tokens for a task or a period, treated as a limited resource to be spent deliberately.

Example: Allocating most of a session's allowance to chapter prose and little to repeated validation runs.

docs.title: Token Cost Estimation
docs.text: Predicting the consumption of a planned task from measured rates, so an author knows the price before committing.

docs.title: Token Cost Model
docs.text: An understanding of what drives consumption — content read, content generated, and overhead paid per agent — used to predict expense before work begins.

docs.title: Token Cost Per Term
docs.text: The average consumption attributable to each glossary entry, useful for estimating the cost of a glossary of any size.

docs.title: Token Frugality Principle
docs.text: The design rule that a workflow should produce required quality at the lowest token cost, so authors on inexpensive plans can complete a book.

docs.title: Token Management Strategies
docs.text: The collected techniques for controlling consumption: file separation, script substitution, gate short-circuiting, and selective reading.

docs.title: Token Usage Dashboard
docs.text: A generated report that presents consumption and duration per skill so expensive steps can be identified.

docs.title: Token Waste Antipatterns
docs.text:
Recurring practices that consume tokens without improving results, such as unnecessary parallel agents or manual assembly of sortable data.

Example: Emitting a sorted glossary through repeated edit calls instead of sorting it with three lines of code.

docs.title: Tokenization
docs.text: The process of splitting raw text into the discrete units a language model consumes. The chosen split determines how much of a document fits into a fixed budget.

docs.title: Tokens Per Minute Limit
docs.text: A cap on throughput, distinct from a total allowance, that governs how quickly work may proceed.

docs.title: Tool Use by Agents
docs.text: The mechanism by which a model requests actions in the outside world — reading a file, running a command, searching the web — and receives the results as new input.

docs.title: Topics Excluded From Scope
docs.text:
An explicit list of subjects a course does not address, preventing generated material from drifting beyond its intended boundary.

Example: Declaring that model training is out of scope stops chapters from expanding into machine learning theory.

docs.title: Trigger Keyword Table
docs.text:
An explicit mapping from request phrases to the action or guide that should handle them, making routing decisions predictable.

Example: The words "timeline" and "chronological" route a request to the timeline generator rather than the chart generator.

docs.title: trim-padding-from-image.py
docs.text: The program that removes surrounding blank space from a picture so it aligns correctly when placed.

docs.title: Understand Level
docs.text: The cognitive category covering construction of meaning, expressed by actions such as explaining, summarizing, and classifying.

docs.title: update-mkdocs-nav.py Script
docs.text: The program that inserts newly created pages into the site menu, ensuring generated content is reachable.

docs.title: URL Verification
docs.text: Confirming that a cited web address resolves and contains the material attributed to it.

docs.title: validate-learning-graph.py
docs.text: The program that checks a generated graph file against its formal schema and reports any structural violation.

docs.title: validate-sims.py Script
docs.text: The program that checks simulations against structural standards and reports violations.

docs.title: Vendor Extension Fields
docs.text:
Metadata keys outside the published specification, added by a particular platform. Some clients ignore them and some reject them outright.

Example: A model: key is understood by one platform and may cause a hard error on another.

docs.title: Venn Diagram Generator
docs.text: The route that produces overlapping-set illustrations showing shared and exclusive membership between categories.

docs.title: Verbatim Text Prompt
docs.text: An image instruction requiring that supplied wording be reproduced exactly, with no paraphrase or substitution.

docs.title: Verbose Output Mode
docs.text: An option that makes a program report its intermediate steps, used for diagnosis.

docs.title: Verified Infographic Pipeline
docs.text: A staged process producing a factual poster in which claims are planned, sourced, verified, and locked before a single image is generated, and the result is audited afterward.

docs.title: Version Control Basics
docs.text:
The practice of recording successive states of a project so any prior state can be recovered and any change can be attributed.

Example: A regenerated glossary can be compared against the previous version to confirm exactly which definitions changed.

docs.title: Virtual Environment
docs.text: An isolated Python installation for a single project, preventing its dependencies from conflicting with those of other projects.

docs.title: vis-network JSON Format
docs.text: The specific arrangement of nodes, edges, and groups expected by the JavaScript library that renders an interactive diagram.

docs.title: vis-network Library
docs.text: A JavaScript library that renders nodes and connecting arrows as an interactive diagram with physics-based layout.

docs.title: vis-timeline Library
docs.text: A JavaScript library that renders dated events along a navigable horizontal axis.

docs.title: Visual Layout Review
docs.text: Inspecting a rendered simulation for presentation defects such as overlapping elements, clipped labels, or controls positioned off-screen.

docs.title: Visual Studio Code
docs.text: A source code editor with integrated terminal, extension support, and file navigation, commonly used for authoring textbook content.

docs.title: Visualization Library Routing
docs.text:
Selecting the rendering technology best matched to a request, based on the kind of data and interaction described.

Example: Chronological events route to a timeline library while node relationships route to a network library.

docs.title: Voltage and Current Scope
docs.text: A display panel plotting electrical quantities over time alongside a simulated circuit.

docs.title: VS Code Terminal
docs.text: A command-line shell embedded in the editor window, allowing commands to be run without leaving the authoring environment.

docs.title: Wikimedia Commons Sourcing
docs.text: Obtaining reusable illustrations and photographs from a large repository of openly licensed media.

docs.title: Wikipedia as a Source
docs.text: Use of an encyclopedic reference as a reliable starting point, placed before specialized sources in a citation list.

docs.title: Word Count Metric
docs.text: The total quantity of written text in a book, used as a basic measure of scale.

docs.title: Worked Examples
docs.text: Fully solved illustrations that show each step of a procedure, used to build competence before independent practice.

docs.title: Writing a Skill Description
docs.text:
Composing the summary that determines when a skill activates, stating both what it does and the situations that should invoke it.

Example: Naming concrete trigger phrases such as "breadboard" and "wiring diagram" makes activation dependable.

docs.title: YAML Frontmatter
docs.text: A block of key-value metadata at the start of a file, delimited by triple dashes, that carries structured information separate from the body.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
This textbook draws upon the following high-quality resources:

  1. Introducing Claude 4 - 2025-05-22 - Anthropic - Official announcement of Claude Opus 4 and Claude Sonnet 4, setting new standards for coding, advanced reasoning, and AI agents, with Claude Opus 4 described as the world's best coding model.

  2. Claude Developer Platform - Release Notes - 2025-11-03 - Anthropic - Official Claude documentation including release notes for the Claude API, client SDKs, and Claude Console, providing comprehensive documentation for developers working with Claude.

  3. Prompting Best Practices - Claude Docs - 2025-11-03 - Anthropic - Comprehensive guide to prompt engineering techniques specifically for Claude 4.x models, covering explicit instructions, long-horizon reasoning, context awareness, and tool usage patterns.

  4. The Ultimate Guide to Prompt Engineering in 2025 - 2025-08-28 - Lakera - Contemporary guide addressing prompt engineering practices for modern AI models including GPT-4o, Claude 4, and Gemini 1.5 Pro, covering seven distinct prompt types and adversarial prompting vulnerabilities.

  5. Prompt Engineering Guide - 2025-11-03 - Prompt Engineering Guide - Comprehensive educational resource covering the latest papers, advanced prompting techniques, model-specific guides, and practical applications including zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, RAG, and ReAct methodologies.

  6. Material for MkDocs - 2025-11-03 - Martin Donath - Official documentation for Material for MkDocs, a powerful documentation framework that makes sharing knowledge easier and more beautiful, trusted by over 50,000 individuals and organizations for creating educational content.

  7. Material for MkDocs - GitHub Repository - 2025-11-01 - Martin Donath - Official GitHub repository for Material for MkDocs with 25,000+ stars, demonstrating widespread adoption by major organizations including AWS, Google, Microsoft, Netflix, and Uber for documentation creation.

  8. Bloom's Taxonomy - Wikipedia - 2025-11-03 - Wikipedia - Comprehensive overview of Bloom's Taxonomy including the 2001 revision that renamed and reordered cognitive levels as Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create, fundamental for educational content design.

  9. Bloom's Revised Taxonomy - 2025-11-03 - Colorado College - Educational resource explaining the six cognitive levels from Anderson and Krathwohl's 2001 revision with specific action verbs for each level to help educators craft effective learning outcomes.

  10. Exploring Knowledge Graphs for the Identification of Concept Prerequisites - 2019-10-01 - Smart Learning Environments - Academic research presenting a methodology that combines semantic web exploration with supervised machine learning to identify concept prerequisites using knowledge graphs, achieving 76-96% precision across multiple domains.

  11. p5.js Education Resources - 2025-11-03 - Processing Foundation - Official directory of p5.js teaching materials, workshops, and curricula from educators worldwide, demonstrating how to use p5.js for creating interactive educational simulations in mathematics, physics, and computer science.

  12. ISO/IEC 11179 - Metadata Registry Standard - 2025-11-03 - Wikipedia - Comprehensive overview of the international standard for representing metadata in a metadata registry, documenting standardization and registration of metadata to make data understandable and shareable across organizations.

  13. Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) - 2025-11-03 - Wikipedia - Thorough coverage of DAG theory including mathematical properties, computational algorithms, and applications in scheduling systems, data processing networks, version control, and citation networks with 57 academic citations.

  14. DAG Algorithms - Neo4j Graph Data Science - 2025-11-03 - Neo4j - Technical documentation for DAG algorithms in the Neo4j GDS library, covering topological sort and longest path algorithms essential for modeling dependencies between entities in learning graphs.

  15. Git Version Control Best Practices - 2025-11-03 - GitLab - Comprehensive guide to version control best practices including incremental changes, atomic commits, branch development, descriptive commit messages, code reviews, and branching strategies for collaborative development.

  16. The Key Principles of Instructional Design (2025) - 2025-11-03 - Devlin Peck - Educational resource covering foundational instructional design theories including behaviorism, cognitive psychology, constructivism, Gagné's Nine Events of Instruction, Mayer's Multimedia Learning Principles, ADDIE model, and Bloom's Taxonomy.

  17. The Ultimate Guide to AI-Assisted Educational Content Creation - 2025-11-03 - Fora Soft - Practical guide to implementing AI tools in educational content creation, covering tool selection, content quality enhancement, personalized learning, and accessibility considerations with evidence showing 20% improvement in test scores.

  18. Documentation for Visual Studio Code - 2025-10-09 - Microsoft - Official VS Code documentation covering setup, configuration, editing features like IntelliSense and Code Actions, debugging capabilities, and language support for developers creating educational content and managing projects.

  19. GitHub Pages Documentation - 2025-11-03 - GitHub - Official documentation for GitHub Pages, a service for hosting static websites directly from GitHub repositories with HTTPS support, ideal for publishing educational textbooks built with MkDocs.

  20. Constructivism as a Theory for Teaching and Learning - 2025-11-03 - Simply Psychology - Comprehensive explanation of constructivism learning theory emphasizing that learners actively build knowledge through experiences and social interactions rather than passively receiving information.

  21. Basic Syntax - Markdown Guide - 2025-11-03 - Markdown Guide - Foundational reference for Markdown syntax covering headings, emphasis, lists, links, images, and code formatting with best practices for compatibility across different Markdown processors.

  22. RFC 8259 - The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format - 2017-12 - IETF - Official Internet Standard specification for JSON, defining the lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format essential for configuration files and data exchange in educational technology projects.

  23. YAML Tutorial: A Complete Language Guide with Examples - 2025-11-03 - Spacelift - Comprehensive tutorial covering YAML fundamentals through advanced topics including syntax, data types, schemas, anchors, aliases, and practical applications in configuration management, infrastructure-as-code, and CI/CD pipelines.

  24. Dublin Core - Metadata Standard - 2025-11-03 - Wikipedia - Overview of the Dublin Core metadata standard (ISO 15836, IETF RFC 5013, ANSI/NISO Z39.85) comprising 15 core metadata elements for describing educational resources, widely adopted for web resources and digital content.

  25. 10 Best Practices for Educational Quizzes in Training - 2025-11-03 - Continu - Professional development resource covering quiz design strategies including pre-testing, diverse question formats, immediate feedback, error tolerance, branching scenarios, and real-world relevance for effective educational assessment.

  26. Using Python's pip to Manage Your Projects' Dependencies - 2025-11-03 - Real Python - Beginner-friendly tutorial teaching how to use pip, Python's standard package manager, to install and manage packages from the Python Package Index for educational technology projects.

docs.title: VS Code Setup for Claude Code
VS Code Setup for Claude Code
docs.text: This guide covers how to configure Visual Studio Code to work optimally with Claude Code, including managing the Claude icon in your Activity Bar.

docs.title: Understanding the Claude Code Icon Location
docs.text: Claude Code uses the Activity Bar (the vertical icon bar on the left side of VS Code), not the status bar at the bottom. The Claude Code icon appears as a spark/lightning bolt icon (⚡).

docs.title: Method 1: Drag and Drop
docs.text:
1. Locate the Claude Code spark icon (⚡) in the Activity Bar (left side of VS Code)
  2. Click and drag the icon up or down to reorder it
  3. Release when it's in your preferred position

docs.title: Method 2: Right-Click Menu
docs.text:
1. Right-click on the Claude Code spark icon in the Activity Bar
  2. Select one of the following options:
  3. Move to Top - Places it at the top of the Activity Bar
  4. Move Up - Moves it up one position
  5. Move Down - Moves it down one position

docs.title: Showing/Hiding the Claude Code Icon
docs.text:
If you don't see the Claude Code icon in your Activity Bar:

  1. Right-click anywhere on the Activity Bar
  2. Look for "Claude Code" in the list
  3. Check/uncheck it to show or hide the icon

docs.title: Opening Claude Code Panel Location
docs.text: You can configure where the Claude Code panel opens:

docs.title: Panel Locations
docs.text: Location Description Sidebar Opens in the left sidebar (alongside file explorer) Panel Opens in the bottom panel (alongside terminal) Secondary Sidebar Opens in the right sidebar (VS Code 1.97+)

docs.title: Changing Panel Location
docs.text:
1. Open Claude Code by clicking the spark icon
  2. Right-click on the Claude Code tab header
  3. Select "Move to..." and choose your preferred location

Or drag the Claude Code tab to your preferred panel area.

docs.title: Default Shortcuts
docs.text: Action Mac Windows/Linux Open Claude Code Click spark icon Click spark icon Toggle Panel Cmd + J Ctrl + J Toggle Sidebar Cmd + B Ctrl + B

docs.title: Setting a Custom Shortcut
docs.text:
1. Open Keyboard Shortcuts:
  2. Mac: Cmd + K, then Cmd + S
  3. Windows/Linux: Ctrl + K, then Ctrl + S
  4. Search for "Claude"
  5. Click the + icon next to the command you want to customize
  6. Press your desired key combination
  7. Press Enter to save

docs.title: Workspace Trust
docs.text:
When opening a new project, VS Code may ask about workspace trust. Claude Code requires a trusted workspace to function fully.

  • Click "Yes, I trust the authors" for projects you're working on
  • Restricted mode limits Claude Code's capabilities

docs.title: Terminal Integration
docs.text:
Claude Code works best with proper terminal access. Ensure your default terminal is configured:

{
    "terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.osx": "zsh",
    "terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.windows": "PowerShell",
    "terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.linux": "bash"
}

Add these to your .vscode/settings.json or user settings.

docs.title: Claude Code Icon Not Visible
docs.text:
1. Check extension is installed:
  2. Open Extensions panel (Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + X)
  3. Search for "Claude Code"

  4. Ensure it's installed and enabled

  5. Check Activity Bar visibility:

  6. Right-click on Activity Bar

  7. Ensure "Claude Code" is checked

  8. Reload VS Code:

  9. Open Command Palette (Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + P)
  10. Type: Developer: Reload Window

docs.title: Extension Not Working
docs.text:
1. Check authentication: Claude Code requires authentication with your Anthropic account
  2. Check workspace trust: Ensure the workspace is trusted
  3. Check for updates: Update the extension to the latest version

docs.title: Panel Opens in Wrong Location
docs.text:
1. Right-click the Claude Code tab header
  2. Select "Move to..." and choose your preferred location
  3. VS Code remembers this preference for future sessions

docs.title: Recommended VS Code Settings
docs.text:
Add these to your .vscode/settings.json for an optimal experience:

{
    "editor.formatOnSave": true,
    "files.autoSave": "afterDelay",
    "files.autoSaveDelay": 1000,
    "terminal.integrated.scrollback": 10000
}
